Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Vignette:
Rodrigo is a 40-year-old Colombian American surgeon, married, and currently practicing at a regional medical center in the southeastern United States. He presented for psychological evaluation approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic wildfire that swept through the rural mountain community where he and his wife had been vacationing to celebrate their fifteenth wedding anniversary. He arrived at the intake appointment in pressed clothes and with the composed affect of a man accustomed to performing competence under pressure, though his PCL-5 score of 49 and the quiet unraveling visible beneath that composure told a more complicated story.

The fire moved faster than any of the emergency alerts had indicated. Rodrigo and his wife had been asleep when the smell reached them — something acrid and dense that he initially mistook for a neighbor's firepit. By the time he understood what it was, the ridge above the rental cabin was already orange. What followed was a chaotic evacuation through smoke so thick he could not see more than a few feet ahead. He remembers the heat, the roar of the fire sounding like sustained thunder rolling without pause, and the moment he lost sight of his wife in the darkness before finding her again near the car. There are stretches of that night he cannot account for — whole segments between leaving the cabin and arriving at the evacuation center that feel simply absent, as though the film of his memory was cut and spliced. He described this incompleteness with visible distress, not because he feared what he might have done, but because the gaps felt like evidence that something in him had broken. When he does remember — when the memory surfaces fully and without invitation — what arrives alongside it is not fear so much as a devastating grief, a sense of loss so total it seems to have no specific object.

In the months that followed, the triggers he had not anticipated proved to be the most disruptive ones. Rodrigo works in an operating environment that is, on its surface, controlled and sterile. But cauterizing tissue produces a smell — faint, burnt, organic — and on three separate occasions since returning to work, that smell has pulled him out of the present moment entirely and returned him to the hillside. The first time it happened he was mid-procedure, and he paused long enough that a scrub technician asked if he was all right. He said he was, finished the operation without incident, and told no one what had actually occurred. He has since developed a habit of slightly increasing ventilation requests in the OR, telling colleagues it is a preference for airflow. Loud sounds carry the same ambush quality — a metal instrument tray dropped in a corridor, a door slamming in the surgical wing — and each one lands in his body before his mind can contextualize it.

Outside of work, Rodrigo had gradually reduced the activities that brought him into contact with anything that might carry smoke or fire smell — backyard gatherings, restaurants with open kitchens, the fireplace his wife had always loved on winter evenings. His wife noticed the fireplace had not been lit since they returned, and when she raised it gently, he changed the subject. He had not explained to her the full weight of what he was carrying. To manage the tension that accumulated across his days, he had begun drinking more regularly in the evenings — a habit he framed to himself as unwinding — and had increasingly turned to sexual fantasy and activity as a means of discharging a restlessness he could not otherwise name. He recognized neither as solutions, but both offered a temporary interruption of something that had no clear off switch.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a conversation with a colleague who had noticed his distraction during a department meeting — not the first such comment in recent months. He had begun to fear, with the particular dread of someone whose identity is built around precision and reliability, that he was becoming a liability in the OR. What he most hopes for, he said carefully, is to be able to walk back into that room and be fully present. What he most fears is that the version of himself who could do that no longer exists.
